title: Human Kidney Anatomy: Cortex, Medulla & Renal Bloodflow
description: Learn human kidney anatomy from the fibrous capsule and renal cortex to medullary pyramids, calyces, the renal pelvis, and nephron filtration blood supply.
h1: Human Kidney Anatomy: Renal Cortex, Medulla, Calyces and Vessels
blurb: Retroperitoneal filtration powerhouses: outer renal cortex, medullary pyramids, calyces, and a million nephrons that purify blood plasma and balance body water.
lead: Tucked behind the peritoneum on either side of the spine, the two bean-shaped kidneys filter the entire plasma volume dozens of times a day to keep body fluids balanced. In this illustrated guide to human kidney anatomy, we examine 20 documented structures—including fibrous capsule, renal cortex, renal pyramid, renal papilla—linking regional topography, tissue architecture, physiological mechanisms, and clinical reasoning.
overview: Tucked behind the peritoneum on either side of the spine, the two bean-shaped kidneys filter the entire plasma volume dozens of times a day to keep body fluids balanced. Each kidney filters about 180 litres of plasma a day and returns all but 1–2 litres to the blood. Filtration happens in the renal corpuscle, where glomerular capillaries sit inside Bowman's capsule. The filtrate then passes through the proximal tubule (bulk reabsorption), the loop of Henle (concentration by countercurrent multiplication), the distal tubule (hormone-controlled fine tuning) and the collecting duct (final water handling under vasopressin). Nephrons drain via the papilla into minor and major calyces, the renal pelvis and the ureter. Within the human body, the kidney (Ren) is situated in retroperitoneal, T12–L3 (left slightly higher), receives arterial perfusion via renal artery from the abdominal aorta — 20–25% of cardiac output, and is innervated by renal plexus (sympathetic T10–L1) — mainly vasomotor.

The fibrous capsule (Capsula fibrosa) is a tough transparent layer of collagenous tissue directly on the kidney surface, surrounded by perinephric fat. Physiologically, the fibrous capsule protects the parenchyma and maintains its shape. The renal cortex (Cortex renalis) is the outer 1 cm, containing all the renal corpuscles, the proximal and distal convoluted tubules, and cortical tissue dipping between pyramids as the renal columns. Physiologically, the renal cortex governs site of blood filtration and most solute reabsorption. The renal pyramid (Pyramides renales) is 8–18 cone-shaped regions of medulla, striped by the straight loops of Henle, vasa recta and collecting ducts that run through them. Physiologically, the renal pyramid governs create and exploit the osmotic gradient that concentrates urine. The renal papilla (Papilla renalis) is the apex of each pyramid, pierced by dozens of duct openings (area cribrosa) that empty into a minor calyx. Physiologically, the renal papilla governs the final exit point for urine from the nephron system. Structurally, the minor & major calyces (Calices renales) comprises cup-like minor calyces (8–18) receive urine from papillae and join into 2–3 major calyces that funnel into the renal pelvis. Physiologically, the minor & major calyces collect urine and conduct it to the pelvis; their smooth muscle helps propel it. The renal pelvis (Pelvis renalis) is the funnel-shaped expansion of the upper ureter inside the hilum. Physiologically, the renal pelvis collects urine from the major calyces and channels it into the ureter.

Clinically, regarding the fibrous capsule, it does not stretch: swelling inside the capsule in acute inflammation causes the dull loin pain of pyelonephritis. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the renal cortex, thinning or scarring of the cortex on ultrasound indicates chronic kidney disease. In clinical pathology involving the renal pyramid, their striated appearance is lost in medullary cystic disease and in the scarring of chronic reflux nephropathy. Medical evaluation of the renal papilla also notes that analgesic abuse, diabetes and sickle-cell disease can cause papillary necrosis, with sloughed tissue in the urine.

questions.question: What do the kidneys do?
questions.answer: Kidneys filter blood, return most water and useful solutes to circulation, and excrete wastes in urine. They also help regulate electrolytes, blood pressure and acid-base balance.

questions.question: How does urine travel from the kidney to the bladder?
questions.answer: Filtrate passes through nephron tubules and collecting ducts into the calyces and renal pelvis; a ureter then carries urine to the bladder.

questions.question: What is the renal cortex?
questions.answer: The renal cortex is the kidney’s outer region. It contains renal corpuscles and most proximal and distal convoluted tubules, and extends between medullary pyramids as renal columns.

questions.question: Where is the renal corpuscle (glomerulus and Bowman’s capsule) located?
questions.answer: The renal corpuscle—glomerulus enclosed by Bowman’s capsule—is located in the kidney cortex.

questions.question: What is the function of the loop of Henle?
questions.answer: The loop of Henle builds the medullary osmotic gradient that helps concentrate urine through countercurrent multiplication.
